Around that time, your melatonin levels drop naturally. If you’re consistently waking up in those early hours, it’s likely that you’re running out of melatonin because you stayed up too late for your body’s natural rhythm.

So if you’re tired of those 3 a.m. wake-ups, don’t fight your biology.. work with it! Get morning sunlight to anchor your rhythm, dim lights at night, and honor your body’s clock.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
One of the reasons I focus so much on dietary carbohydrates is that no nutrient in the blood is as volatile as glucose. It can climb sharply within minutes of a meal and fall just as quickly. And as much as the blood sugar spike after a meal gets most of the attention, when it comes to hunger, the drop that follows may matter more.

In a study of more than a thousand people wearing continuous glucose monitors, researchers looked at what happened to blood sugar in the hours after eating and how hungry people felt afterward. The size of the spike wasn't the best predictor of hunger. The dip was.

Some people's glucose rose after a meal and then settled back to where it started. Others rose and then fell below their starting level about two to three hours later. That second group, the "big dippers," got hungrier sooner, ate their next meal earlier, and took in more calories over the rest of the day.

This helps explain a common experience. Someone eats a breakfast of cereal, toast, or a pastry, feels fine for a while, and then by mid-morning is hungry again and looking for a snack. It isn't a lack of willpower. Their blood sugar went up quickly and then came down below where it began, and the body responds to that drop by pushing them to eat.

It also shows why the same meal can affect people so differently. One person's glucose barely dips after a bowl of oatmeal, while another's crashes. This is one more reason a glucose monitor is so useful. It shows not only how high a meal sends your glucose, but how far it falls afterward.

Meals built around protein and fat, with fewer refined carbohydrates, tend to produce a smaller rise and a gentler return, which means less of a dip and steadier hunger.

If someone keeps feeling hungry a couple of hours after eating, it's worth looking at whether that meal is sending their blood sugar up and then down below where it started.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
A high A1C doesn't always mean high blood sugar. This matters, because A1C is the number most people and many doctors rely on to judge glucose control and to diagnose diabetes.

A1C measures how much glucose has attached to hemoglobin, the protein inside red blood cells. Glucose sticks to hemoglobin slowly and steadily, so the longer a red blood cell stays in circulation, the more glucose builds up on it. That's why A1C is treated as a two- to three-month average of blood sugar.

That also means A1C depends on more than glucose. It depends on how old the red blood cells are. When iron is low, the body makes fewer new red blood cells, so the cells already in circulation are older on average. Older cells have had more time to collect glucose, and A1C goes up even though blood sugar hasn't changed.

When researchers pooled the studies in adults without diabetes, iron deficiency, with or without anemia, was consistently linked to a higher A1C. Some other types of anemia, where red blood cells are destroyed faster than usual, can do the opposite and make A1C look falsely low.

This matters most for people who are more likely to be low in iron, including menstruating women, pregnant women, frequent blood donors, and people who eat little or no meat. In these groups, an A1C in the prediabetes range might reflect iron status as much as glucose.

If someone's A1C doesn't line up with their fasting glucose or glucose monitor readings, it's worth checking iron status before concluding that blood sugar is the problem.

That matters most for people low in iron, like frequent blood donors or people who eat little or no meat.

If your A1C doesn't match your fasting glucose, ask your doctor to check your iron too.

hits.text:
Statins & Dementia: What Happened When They Stopped (Then Restarted) the Drugs
In a 2012 pilot study (Padala et al., American Journal of Geriatric Pharmacotherapy), researchers took 18 older adults with Alzheimer’s who were already on statins and ran a simple test:
•  Stopped the statins for 6 weeks
•  Restarted them for another 6 weeks
What they found:
•  Cognition improved when the statins were stopped (MMSE scores rose ~1.9 points, P = 0.014).
•  Cognition worsened again when the statins were restarted (MMSE dropped ~1.9 points, P = 0.007).
•  Cholesterol rose off the drug and fell when it was restarted (as expected).
•  There were also trends toward better daily function (ADL/IADL) while off the statins.
The authors concluded that statins may adversely affect cognition in people with dementia. This was a small, open-label pilot (not a large randomized controlled trial), so it doesn’t prove causation for everyone—but the withdrawal/rechallenge design makes the signal hard to ignore.
Cholesterol is critical for brain function. Some statins (especially lipophilic ones) can cross the blood-brain barrier and may interfere with that. The FDA has long noted reversible cognitive side effects with statins.
This doesn’t mean every patient should stop their statin. It does raise the question of whether continued use is always the right call in someone already dealing with dementia—especially if the original indication was primary prevention. 
Source: Padala KP et al. Am J Geriatr Pharmacother. 2012;10(5):296-302. PMID: 22921881

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Calories in, calories out has some merit. Energy balance is real. But it treats a calorie as a calorie no matter when it's eaten, and the body doesn't work that way.

In a study of healthy young adults, people ate the exact same dinner on two different occasions, once at 6 PM and once at 10 PM. The food was identical, the rest of the day's eating was identical, and they went to bed at the same time. By the CICO math, nothing changed.

But the body handled that dinner differently. After the late dinner, blood sugar ran higher in the hours afterward, and the body burned less of the fat from that meal while they slept. The same calories went in, but what the body did with them changed simply because of the clock.

The late dinner also raised cortisol, a stress hormone that tends to push blood sugar up. And the effects were strongest in people who naturally go to bed earlier, which points to the body's internal clock. As the evening goes on, insulin doesn't work as well, and the body is less ready for a large meal.

This is one of the main problems with counting calories alone. The number on the label tells you what went in, but it can't tell you how the body will use it. Timing, hormones, and the body's clock all shape whether that energy gets burned or stored.

If someone is relying on calorie counting alone, it's worth remembering that when those calories are eaten can change what the body does with them.

Is this why our food is making us sick? 

In 1958, Congress created a narrow exemption so everyday ingredients like salt, vinegar, and baking soda could skip the full formal review process required for new food additives. The idea was simple: if something had a long history of safe use and was generally recognized as safe by experts, it did not need the same premarket scrutiny. Decades later, that modest exception has become the main route for most new substances entering the American food supply.

Under the modern GRAS system, a company can decide on its own that a chemical or novel ingredient is safe. It is not required to notify the FDA, let alone wait for approval. Even when a company does submit a voluntary notice, it can withdraw the filing if the agency raises questions and still put the ingredient on the market. Estimates suggest hundreds of substances have entered foods this way with little or no independent review. Analyses show that roughly 99 percent of new food chemicals introduced since 2000 used the GRAS pathway rather than the formal additive petition process. 

Safety assessments are frequently conducted by people with clear financial ties to the manufacturer—company employees, paid consultants, or expert panels selected by the company itself. Studies of hundreds of GRAS notices have found conflicts of interest nearly ubiquitous. A small circle of recurring experts has dominated many of these panels for years. The FDA has issued guidance intended to reduce bias, yet independent analyses indicate it is often ignored. 

The practical result is limited transparency. The agency lacks a complete public inventory of every self-affirmed GRAS substance, the amounts used, or the specific foods involved. Cumulative exposure from multiple related chemicals is rarely evaluated. When problems surface later, post-market action has historically been slow. 

A former senior FDA official once acknowledged that the agency simply does not have the information needed to vouch for the safety of many of these substances.
This is not a technical quirk. It is a structural shift that places primary responsibility for determining what is safe in the hands of the companies that profit from the ingredients. 

Consumers and independent researchers are left with incomplete data about what is actually in the food supply and why it was allowed there. For substances with centuries of ordinary culinary use, the original intent of the law still makes sense. For the steady stream of newer chemicals entering through the same door, the shortcomings are harder to ignore.

Losing body fat is good for health. But there is a side of it that rarely gets mentioned.

Many pollutants we pick up from the environment, like older pesticides and industrial chemicals called organochlorines, dissolve in fat. Once they are in the body, they get stored in fat tissue and can stay there for years.

When fat is broken down for energy during weight loss, some of these stored chemicals come back out into the blood.

In one study, adults with obesity followed a reduced-calorie diet for 15 weeks. Afterward, every organochlorine the researchers detected was higher in the blood. The more weight people lost, the bigger the rise.

Another study looked at people who lost weight by dieting or after bariatric surgery. Blood levels of these chemicals went up in both groups. A year after surgery, people had lost nearly half their body weight, and total levels in the blood had risen almost fivefold. The rise matched how much weight was lost.

This matters because these chemicals aren't harmless. A separate study found that people with higher amounts of certain stored pesticides in their fat had a greater risk of developing metabolic problems over 10 years.

This is not a reason to avoid losing weight. In a sense, fat tissue has been doing a protective job by keeping these chemicals away from more sensitive organs. And researchers still don't know whether the temporary rise in the blood causes long-term harm.

If someone is losing a large amount of weight, especially quickly, it's worth knowing that what was stored in their fat doesn't simply disappear. It passes through the blood on the way out.

Dr. David Unwin is a UK GP in Southport who has pioneered low-carbohydrate approaches for type 2 diabetes in primary care since around 2013. Patients typically cut starchy and sugary foods and increase whole foods including meat, fish, eggs, and full-fat dairy—raising protein and fat while lowering carbs. 
Traditional concerns (based largely on older theory about protein-induced hyperfiltration) suggested higher protein might harm kidneys, especially in people with diabetes who are at higher risk of CKD. Unwin and colleagues reviewed the evidence and analyzed real-world data from his practice. 
In a 2021 paper covering 143 patients with T2D (mostly normal renal function or mild CKD) followed for an average of ~30 months on the low-carb approach:
•  Serum creatinine improved by a mean of 4.7 μmol/L (statistically significant).
•  Other renal markers and cardiovascular risk factors (weight, HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids) also improved in the majority.
•  This occurred instead of the expected age- and diabetes-related decline. 
Unwin has noted that controlling hyperglycemia (a key driver of diabetic kidney damage) appears more protective than restricting protein in this context. He continues to encourage protein-rich foods from meat, eggs, and fish while monitoring patients. The data is strongest for people with normal or mildly reduced kidney function; effects in moderate-to-severe CKD remain less certain, and guidelines still often recommend caution or protein moderation in advanced disease.

virals.name: @levelsio
virals.text:
My vlog today was fully edited by Claude Code with Opus 5.5!

I copied the video clips from my DJI to a folder, then opened Claude Code in it and asked it to edit it into a 10 minute vlog

I made a few adjustments but not a lot

It transcribed everything I said with mlx-whisper (Whisper large-v3-turbo running on my MacBook Pro's GPU through Apple's MLX)

It pulled video frames every few seconds into grid images (contact sheets), so Claude could see what's in each clip

It used SpeechBrain ECAPA (a voice-matching model) to figure out what was my voice from other people

It then made thumbnails with OpenCV with YuNet's face detector

The edit itself is a list of cuts in a JSON file: which clip, start time, end time, Claude then picked the pieces by reading the transcripts and looking at the frame grids by itself

I added on screen captions for X and on YouTube for the first minute with Pillow (Python's image library)

P.S. I didn't ask for any of this, and I didn't know any of this until @thesamparr just asked me how I edited it

All I asked for was "Claude can you edit these clips into a 10 minute vlog for X and YouTube"

I think if I didn't have AI to edit it, I wouldn't be vlogging because editing would be such a painful and slow process for me and hiring someone to do it would be even more hassle for me!

virals.text:
I decompiled probably my favorite game ever: Battlefield 1942 and I put it on the web with multiplayer for you to play here:

👉 https://t.co/6C8H8KtSaU 👈

(It's the free shareware demo)

It was way harder than the other ports like Quake and DOOM I did because they already had lots of open source projects and work behind them

In case of Battlefield 1942 there was literally absolutely nothing to work on top of, nobody had ever ported it and there was no open source engine for it, nor did the makers ever open source it (like id Software did with Quake 3)

I tried it 6 months ago and essentiay gave up but I tried it today again with Opus 5.5 asking "can you try port the BF1942 demo in this folder to web"

So me and Claude Code (well let's be honest mostly Claude Code) did crazy shit today:
- it disassembled the x86 raw machine code to find 57,000 x86 functions
- it translated each x86 function into a C function (mov eax, [esi+0x110] becomes eax = READ32(esi + 0x110), I have no idea what any of this means btw)
- it outputed 100,000 lines of C
- it then compiled that to WebAsswmbly with Emscripten
- there were 300x Windows and Direct3D functions used which we had to rewrite to WebGL 2 and OpenGL to work on the web
- then we had to build our own network stack so it could connect to our multiplayer server via WebSockets

I have no idea how it did any of this but it did it and it seems to work! 😊 

Come play and report any bugs here!
